abstract: T. Harvey: The film which Mr Symes has shown probably shows up more clearly than any verbal description the outstanding ease of control of the differential locomotive. The most convincing experience of all, however, is actually to drive the loco as a number of people have already done. Being privileged to assist Mr Symes in the long series of tests which were carried out I have been able to observe the reactions of these visitors. Invariably the pattern was the same; an extremely sceptical outlook when first told about the loco and what it could do; a smile of contempt when they first saw the strange contraption in its shed; and finally overwhelming enthusiasm when they had put it through its paces. The treatment it received was unmerciful — and we encouraged visitors to try the most vicious driving tricks they could think up. I have lost count of the number of times the controller was thrown from full speed forward to full speed reverse while the loco was pulling its maximum load — often on a downgrade at that. The fact that the experimental loco is still running without any need of an overhaul is more revealing as regards its inherent ruggedness than all the theory in the world. I hope that the prototype and production locos will never be driven the way the experimental loco has been, but if they are they will take it in their stride.

abstract: Professor A. F. P. J. Heydorn (Member): Mr Rippon's paper takes the reader into one of the fields of heavy current engineering newly explored during the past two decades. Impulse testing of transformers is, like many other recent subjects of electric power research, accessible to the equipment and the material available only in the biggest of industrial laboratories and undertakings. This is in striking contrast to the light current field, where a laboratory arrangement comprising comparatively cheap and simple equipment may have equal scientific and technical importance as a heavy current set-up costing many thousands of pounds. Perhaps it is this remoteness of the battlefield of heavy current progress which causes students in electrical engineering to follow the lure of the light current side to such an extent that some overseas power undertakings complain of being starved out of the rising generation of engineers.

This paper illustrates, once again, that whilst lightning is undoubtedly the most formidable enemy of both the power and communication engineer, the more information which is sought and obtained on its many vagaries the more confident engineers become in applying measures to minimise its damaging effects and the authors are to be congratulated on a very thorough study of the subject and on the manner in which this has been applied. We also consider that the large amount of detail and fundamental data incorporated in the paper make it a most useful reference for those many who are concerned with lightning generally and with its effects on power or communication circuits in particular.

articleTitle: Author's reply to discussion on germanium power rectifiers
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr Brummer has described the germanium and silicon rectifiers developed in the United States of America. In England too, silicon rectifiers are undergoing intensive development and experimental cells have been produced which are capable of operating at a d.c. output of 1 kW and a junction temperature of 200°C. The low reverse current of a silicon rectifier compared with that of a germanium rectifier does not seem to offer any practical advantage except in so far as it enables higher operating temperatures to be used. The reverse current of the germanium rectifier is already so low that it has little effect on the efficiency or heating. The possibility of detecting a failing silicon rectifier by the increase in reverse current is attractive; a method by which this can be done in an equipment having a large number of cells in series and parallel will be quite interesting to develop.

abstract: Professor J. M. Meek made the point, with which the authors concur, that the distance of 56 feet assumed for the length of a lightning leader side-flash which would approach a transmission line, might not be accurate. The emphasis on average conditions, perhaps, should have been more accentuated, whereby it would have been appreciated that 50 per cent of strokes having greater than average charges were likely to strike a transmission line from greater distances, and vice versa. The average peak current observed was used, together with assumptions as to the wave form, and critical disruptive gradient for air, to apply Golde's analysis, and the authors believe that these assumptions arc substantially correct, in view of the agreement with other observers over the approximate number of lightning strokes to ground. The calculations should, in any case, provide a greater measure of accuracy than so far achieved in evaluating the comparative performance of transmission lines of differing heights.

abstract: In determining insulation levels two factors are of importance. First, the overvoltages which can be produced by the system; second, the limitation of the voltages caused by atmospheric disturbances. The former can, and usually do, control the choice of surge diverter or co-ordinating gap and therefore the efficiency of the limitation of voltages due to lightning and, ultimately, the insulation level of the apparatus. It follows that detailed consideration should always be given to the possible overvoltages which can be generated on a system. Usually, as the result of bitter experience, attention is focused on the most obvious reason for overvoltages, the interruption of current, and it is not always appreciated that excessive voltages can be obtained by simpler mechanisms, for example, circuit unbalances.
